pages.summary: A probability distribution object with the parameters given.
body: The object holds a distribution and its parameters, and goes to the functions that work on any distribution: `pdf`, `cdf`, `icdf`, `random`, `mean`, `median`, `std`, `var`, `iqr` and `truncate`. Its parameters are its properties, so they can be read and changed by name. Parameters left out keep their defaults (the normal's `mu` 0 and `sigma` 1). `makedist` with no input lists the distributions it knows.
syntax: The distribution with its default parameters.

examples.title: A normal distribution and its numbers
examples.code:
pd = makedist('Normal', 'mu', 10, 'sigma', 2)
[mean(pd) std(pd)]
cdf(pd, 12) - cdf(pd, 8)
icdf(pd, 0.975)
examples.output:
pd = 

  NormalDistribution

  Normal distribution
       mu = 10
    sigma = 2


ans =

    10     2

ans =

    0.6827

ans =

   13.9199

examples.title: Its parameters as properties
Densities of three distributions
examples.code:
x = linspace(0, 6, 300);
plot(x, pdf(makedist('Exponential', 'mu', 1), x), ...
     x, pdf(makedist('Gamma', 'a', 3, 'b', 0.7), x), ...
     x, pdf(makedist('Lognormal', 'mu', 0.5, 'sigma', 0.4), x))
legend('exponential', 'gamma', 'lognormal')

pages.summary: A probability distribution object fitted to data.
body: Estimates the distribution's parameters from the data by maximum likelihood (the normal's and lognormal's sigma being the unbiased estimate), and returns an object that knows its data: `paramci` gives the parameters' confidence intervals and `negloglik` the likelihood. `'Kernel'` gives a smooth nonparametric fit instead. With `'By'`, a fit for each group.
syntax: The named distribution fitted to the data `x`.
A fit for each group, in a cell array.

examples.title: A Weibull fit and its intervals
examples.code:
rng default
x = wblrnd(2, 1.5, 200, 1);
pd = fitdist(x, 'Weibull')
paramci(pd)
examples.output:
pd = 

  WeibullDistribution

  Weibull distribution, fitted to 200 values
    A = 1.99037     [1.80943, 2.18941]
    B = 1.53227     [1.37361, 1.70926]


ans =

    1.8094    1.3736
    2.1894    1.7093

examples.title: The fit against the data

pages.summary: Maximum likelihood estimates of a distribution's parameters, with confidence intervals.
body: The parameters that make the data most probable. Without a distribution the data are taken to be normal, and sigma is the likelihood's own (normalized by N, not N-1). The intervals are in two rows, lower ends first.
syntax: The normal mean and standard deviation.
For a named distribution, with confidence intervals.
For the binomial, with the number of trials.

pages.summary: The density, distribution function, quantiles and random numbers of any distribution.
body: Given a distribution object (from `makedist` or `fitdist`), or a distribution's name and its parameters in the order its own function takes them (`normpdf(x, mu, sigma)` becomes `pdf('Normal', x, mu, sigma)`). For a discrete distribution, `pdf` gives the probabilities. `cdf` with `'upper'` gives the probability above `x`.
syntax: The density of the distribution object at `x`.
y = pdf(name, x, A, B, C)
Of a named distribution with its parameters.
An m-by-n array of random numbers (one number without a size).
r = random(name, A, B, C, m, n)

pages.summary: A distribution object limited to an interval, its probability there scaled up to 1.
body: The truncated distribution keeps the shape of the original between `lower` and `upper` and has no probability outside: a normal measurement that cannot be negative, for one. Its random numbers fall in the interval.

pages.summary: The confidence intervals of a fitted distribution object's parameters, and its negative log-likelihood.
body: `paramci` gives an interval for each parameter, lower ends in the first row; `negloglik` the negative log-likelihood of the fit for its data, smaller for a better fit (for comparing distributions fitted to the same data, as with an information criterion).
syntax: 95% intervals, a column for each parameter.

pages.summary: The multivariate normal distribution: its density, its distribution function, and random vectors.
body: Each row of `X` is a point, `mu` the mean (a row) and `Sigma` the covariance matrix; left out, the means are zero and the covariance is the identity. `mvncdf` gives the probability that every component is below the point's, by numerical integration (good to about 1e-5). `mvnrnd` gives a row for each random vector.
syntax: The density at each row of `X`.
The probability below each row of `X`.

pages.summary: The multivariate t distribution: its density, its distribution function, and random vectors.

syntax: The density at each row of `X`.
The probability below each row of `X`.

pages.summary: Random samples: of numbers or values, without replacement unless asked; of the elements or rows of data.
body: `randsample(n, k)` draws `k` of the numbers 1 to n without replacement; given a population, it draws from its values, with replacement when asked and with weights. `datasample` draws elements of a vector or rows of a matrix, with replacement unless `'Replace'` is false, and also returns their indices.
syntax: From the population's values, with or without replacement, with weights `w`.
Without replacement or with weights, and the indices drawn.
